<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Vairōcanaparājayaḥ narrates the story of the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara of Jainism, Vairocana, and his victory over the demon Rāhu. The kāvya begins with a description of the universe and the Jaina cosmology. It then moves on to narrate the story of Rāhu, who had become invincible due to a boon from Lord Brahma. He began tormenting the world by swallowing the sun and the moon, causing eclipses.<br><br>The gods then sought the help of Vairocana, who fought a fierce battle with Rāhu. After several rounds of combat, Vairocana emerged victorious and cut off Rāhu's head with his discus. The kāvya then describes Rāhu's repentance and his subsequent release from the cycle of birth and death.<br><br>The work also includes several stories and legends related to the Jaina religion and philosophy, including the story of King Hariścandra and the concept of karma. It is considered an important work in Jaina literature, particularly for its depiction of the Tīrthaṅkara and their teachings.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Vairōcanaparājayaḥ is a Sanskrit kāvya that narrates the story of the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara of Jainism, Vairocana, and his battle with the demon Rāhu. The work also includes stories and legends related to Jaina religion and philosophy, such as the story of King Hariścandra and the concept of karma. It is considered an important work in Jaina literature.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">The uniqueness of Vairōcanaparājayaḥ lies in its depiction of the Jain concept of the universe and the Jaina cosmology, which is described in detail in the beginning of the work. It also presents the story of the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara, Vairocana, and his victory over the demon Rāhu, which is not commonly found in other Jaina texts. The work is also unique in its use of imagery and metaphors, as well as its poetic style, which makes it an important contribution to Sanskrit literature. Additionally, the work includes several stories and legends related to the Jaina religion and philosophy, making it an important source for the study of Jaina thought and tradition.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Vairōcanaparājayaḥ is considered an important work in Sanskrit literature, particularly in the Jaina tradition. It is a masterpiece of kāvya poetry, showcasing the author's skill in composition, description, and narration. The work is also significant for its depiction of the Jaina cosmology, philosophy, and legends. Its contribution to Sanskrit literature lies in its portrayal of the Tīrthaṅkara, their teachings, and the ideals of the Jaina religion, which enriches our understanding of Indian culture and spirituality.<br><br>One notable aspect of the Vairōcanaparājayaḥ is its use of various poetic techniques and styles. The work employs the use of similes, metaphors, alliteration, and other rhetorical devices, which are typical of Sanskrit poetry. However, the poet also incorporates elements of Prākrit and Apabhramśa languages, which were popular in the region at the time, into his work, creating a unique style of his own. The kāvya also contains several verses that are written in the Chandas meter, which is considered one of the most difficult meters in Sanskrit poetry. The combination of these elements makes the Vairōcanaparājayaḥ a significant contribution to Sanskrit literature and a notable example of the literary culture of medieval India.</div></div></div>
